paragraphs.text: SHAHID BILAL HASSAN, J- Brief facts germane to the filing of the instant appeal are as such that the respondent, Haji Muhammad Ashraf, instituted an ejectment petition against one Nadeem Hussain for seeking possession of House No. 18-A, Street No. 2, Sham Nagar, Raj Garh, Lahore (the “property”), which was accepted on the basis of the latter's conceding statement. Pursuant thereto, possession of the demised premises was delivered to the respondent through the Court Bailiff in execution of the ejectment order. The respondent thereafter alleged that, after possession of the property had been restored to him through the Court Bailiff, the appellants forcibly and unlawfully re-entered the premises and dispossessed him. Consequently, the respondent instituted an application under Sections 144 and 151, C.P.C. seeking restoration of possession of the property (the “application”). Ultimately, vide order dated 15.05.2014, the learned Special Judge (Rent), Lahore allowed the respondent's application ex-parte and directed restoration of possession in his favour. According to the appellants, the respondent initiated proceedings under Sections 144 and 151, C.P.C. through an attorney by impleading a non-entity instead of the appellants, ultimately obtaining possession of the disputed premises despite there being no order against them. Claiming to have acquired knowledge of the ex-parte order passed in the application only on 02.07.2014, the appellants filed an application under Section 12(2), C.P.C., which was dismissed on 24.07.2014. The appeal preferred against this order was subsequently dismissed as barred by limitation on 20.09.2014, and Civil Revision No.3009 of 2014 preferred before the Lahore High Court also met the same fate vide judgment dated 23.07.2015.

Leave having already been granted by this Court vide order dated 09.11.2016 in the C.P.L.A. preferred by the present appellants, this appeal is to be decided in the light of the following observations made by this Court in the leave granting order: "It prima facie transpires that the respondents when failed to get ejectment of the petitioners in two rounds of litigation, initiated yet another litigation by showing the Attorney to be Applicant and a non-entity as respondent without impleading the petitioners and having obtained a consent order, took possession of the demised premises from the petitioners in its execution, notwithstanding such order was never passed against them. The case went up and down and was eventually remanded to the lower forum for decision afresh, Again petitioner was proceeded against ex-parte. An application under Section 12(2) CPC was filed by the petitioners, but same was dismissed. It may be a case of comedy of errors as far as the petitioner is concerned but the fact is that respondent has not approached the Court of law with clean hands. We, therefore, like to scrutinize the entire record and thus grant leave in this case to consider the points mentioned above."

Learned counsel for the appellants contended that the respondent had abused the process of the Court by initiating proceedings under Sections 144 and 151, C.P.C. without impleading the appellants, despite being fully aware that they were in possession of the disputed property. It was argued that the respondent procured an ex parte order against a non-entity through concealment of material facts and thereafter obtained possession of the disputed property in execution thereof. Learned counsel submitted that the proceedings were vitiated by fraud and were liable to be set aside under Section 12(2), C.P.C. He further argued that the Courts below failed to appreciate these material irregularities and erroneously dismissed the appellants' challenge on technical grounds of limitation without examining the illegality underlying the proceedings. Reliance was placed upon the observations contained in the leave granting order.

Conversely, learned counsel for the respondent supported the impugned judgment and argued that possession of the disputed property had originally been restored to the respondent through the Court Bailiff in execution of a lawful ejectment order, whereafter the appellants unlawfully and forcibly reoccupied the premises. It was submitted that the application under Sections 144 and 151, C.P.C. was, therefore, rightly entertained to restore the respondent to the position from which he had been illegally dispossessed. Learned counsel further contended that the appellants had failed to challenge the ex parte order within the prescribed period of limitation and had not furnished any satisfactory explanation for the delay. He maintained that the findings recorded by the Courts below were concurrent findings of fact, suffered from no legal infirmity, and warranted no interference by this Court.
We have heard the learned counsel for the parties and have examined the record with their able assistance.

At the very outset we note that the principles governing limitation are too well settled to admit any cavil. The law of limitation is not a mere technical rule of procedure, rather, it is founded upon sound public policy aimed at securing certainty, finality and repose in litigation. Once a valuable right accrues to a successful litigant by efflux of time, the same cannot be disturbed except upon demonstration of sufficient cause within contemplation of law1. Equally settled is the principle that a party seeking condonation of delay must approach the Court with clean hands, disclose all material facts and furnish a plausible, satisfactory and bona fide explanation covering the entire period of delay2. Negligence, indolence or casual conduct do not constitute sufficient cause.

Examined on the touchstone of the above principles, we find no infirmity in the view taken by the learned High Court. The appellants asserted that they acquired knowledge of the ex parte order dated 15.05.2014 on 02.07.2014 and thereafter filed an application under Section 12(2), C.P.C., which came to be dismissed on 24.07.2014. The appeal preferred thereagainst was admittedly filed beyond the prescribed period of limitation and was accompanied by an application seeking condonation of delay. Both the learned appellate Court and the learned High Court concurrently found that the delay had remained unexplained and that no sufficient cause had been shown for invoking the equitable discretion vested in the Court. We have independently examined the explanation furnished by the appellants and find it wholly inadequate. The appellants have failed to account for the delay with the degree of diligence required by law. We, therefore, find ourselves in complete agreement with the concurrent findings recorded by the Courts below that the appeal was hopelessly barred by limitation.

Even otherwise, the conduct of the appellants throughout the litigation does not commend itself to the exercise of equitable jurisdiction. The record reveals that the proceedings under Sections 144 and 151, C.P.C. culminated in an ex parte order dated 15.05.2014. Although the appellants subsequently availed the remedy under Section 12(2), C.P.C., the same was dismissed. Thereafter, instead of diligently pursuing the remedies available under the law, they failed to satisfactorily explain the delay in 1Ramlal and others v. Rewa Coalfields Ltd. (AIR 1962 SC 361); Imtiaz Ali v. Atta Muhammad and another (PLD 2008 Supreme Court 462); Government of Pakistan v. Malbrow Builders Contractor Sialkot (2006 SCMR 1248); Lal Khan through legal heirs v. Muhammad Yousaf through legal heirs (PLD 2011 Supreme Court 657). 2Khushi Muhammad v. Mst. Fazal Bibi (PLD 2016 SC 872); Secretary To Government Of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa Communication And Works Department, Peshawar and others v. Messrs Parcon Associate Government Contractors through Muhammad Haroon and others (PLD 2025 Supreme Court 371); Lal Khan through LRs v. Muhammad Yousaf through LRs (PLD 2011 SC 657). preferring the statutory appeal, which was rightly dismissed as time- barred. The revision petition before the learned High Court also failed on the same ground. Such conduct unmistakably reflects negligence, lack of diligence and a casual approach towards the process of law. A litigant seeking equitable relief must himself exhibit due vigilance, which, in the present case, is conspicuously absent.

Learned counsel for the appellants has laid considerable emphasis on the observations contained in the leave granting order, particularly the allegation that the respondent had initiated proceedings against a non-entity without impleading the appellants and had thereby procured possession of the disputed property. We are mindful of the settled principle that, as far as possible, disputes ought to be adjudicated on their merits and not be defeated on mere technicalities. It is precisely for this reason that, notwithstanding our conclusion that the appellants' challenge was rightly held to be barred by limitation, we have independently scrutinized the entire record within the parameters delineated in the leave granting order. Such scrutiny, however, does not advance the appellants' case. On the contrary, the record lends support to the concurrent findings returned by the Courts below.

Our conclusion is further reinforced by the findings recorded by the learned trial Court while dismissing the appellants' application under Section 12(2), C.P.C. The record reveals that the proceedings under Sections 144 and 151, C.P.C. were initially instituted in the year 2003. The appellants had earlier been proceeded against ex parte and had moved an application under Order IX Rule 7, C.P.C. for setting aside the ex parte proceedings, which was dismissed on 21.01.2013. Although the Appellants successfully challenged that order before the revisional Court and the matter was remanded for a fresh decision, notices were again issued to the appellants after remand. Despite service, they once again failed to appear and were proceeded against ex parte vide orders dated 16.09.2013 and 10.10.2013. The learned trial Court, after examining the entire record, specifically found that the appellants had deliberately avoided the process of the Court, that they had remained aware of the proceedings throughout, having participated in earlier rounds of litigation, and had failed to establish that they were unaware of the proceedings or that no process had been issued upon them. It was further observed that even in the earlier proceedings under Section 12(2), C.P.C. instituted by one Hashmat Bibi, the present appellants had participated by filing a written statement, which too was dismissed. These findings have neither been shown to suffer from any misreading or non-reading of the record nor to be perverse or arbitrary.

In view of the foregoing, we are unable to persuade ourselves that the appellants have made out any case for interference in the concurrent findings recorded by the Courts below. On the contrary, the record demonstrates that repeated opportunities were afforded to the appellants to contest the proceedings, yet they consistently failed to avail the same with due diligence. Their own conduct disentitles them from invoking the equitable jurisdiction of this Court. The findings recorded by the learned Court below, as affirmed by the learned High Court, therefore call for no indulgence by this Court.

We may also observe that the leave granting order merely indicated that the record warranted closer scrutiny and did not constitute any expression of opinion on the merits of the controversy. Having now undertaken that scrutiny, we are satisfied that the learned High Court committed no error in affirming the dismissal of the appellants' challenge. The impugned judgment neither suffers from any misreading or non-reading of the record nor discloses any jurisdictional or legal infirmity calling for interference by this Court.

Consequently, this appeal fails and is dismissed. The impugned judgment dated 23.07.2015 passed by the learned Lahore High Court, as well as the concurrent orders of the Courts below, are affirmed. The appellants, by their persistent negligence and repeated abuse of the judicial process, have compelled the respondent to engage in avoidable and protracted litigation spanning over two decades. Such conduct does not deserve any favourable indulgence rather an exemplary action. Accordingly, the appellants are burdened with costs of Rs.200,000/- (Rupees Two Hundred Thousand only), to be paid to the respondent within thirty (30) days from the date of this judgment, failing which the same shall be recoverable as arrears of land revenue in accordance with law.

Before concluding, we must express our concern over the manner in which a dispute falling within the summary jurisdiction of the Rent Controller has remained pending for almost three decades. Rent statutes constitute a special code intended to secure swift and inexpensive determination of disputes relating to tenancy and possession. When proceedings of such nature are permitted to stroll through successive applications, revisions and appeals for decades, the very purpose for which the legislature carved out a special summary forum stands frustrated. Courts are, therefore, under a corresponding duty to ensure that rent proceedings are not converted into endless civil litigation through dilatory tactics or abuse of process. Delay in such matters not only prejudices the parties but also erodes public confidence in the administration of justice. Therefore, the timespan provided under law for concluding a lis has to be adhered to and unnecessary adjournments as well as applications based on mala fide intentions should and must not be encouraged rather strict action thereon be taken. JUDGE JUDGE JUDGE Announced in open Court on 29.07.2026, at Lahore. JUDGE “Approved for Reporting” M.A. Hassan
